title: Close an inside-fitting pressure cooker
keywords: oval lid through a smaller mouth
instruction: Close the pressure cooker, ready to go on the stove.
context: Inside-fitting (inner-lid) pressure cookers are an everyday pot in millions of homes. The lid is larger than the oval mouth: it goes in only tilted and crosswise, has to be turned in line inside, and falls back into the cooker unless it is pulled up against the rim and the locking loop is put over the handles.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. The table top is the kitchen counter. (1) A 1.5 litre inside-fitting pressure cooker body (Hawkins Classic CL15, 3.25 mm aluminium), loose on the counter, its axis 34 cm forward and 16 cm right of the centre line: a 130 mm flat base, a 159 mm body, its rim's top 105 mm above the counter, with a 3 mm lip running in to an oval mouth 120 x 138 mm (the long axis across the handle). Body 1.04 kg plus 0.40 kg of rice and water, 22 mm deep (real trial: 95 g of uncooked white rice and 300 ml of room-temperature tap water, fresh each session). A black bakelite body handle (130 x 26 x 28 mm, top 102.5 mm above the counter) on a steel bracket points left and toward the robot at 45 degrees; on the bracket, 93 mm from the cooker's axis, a 6 x 10.5 mm steel pivot post with its top 116.5 mm above the counter; under the handle's end, a hook pocket for the locking loop. (2) The lid, 0.21 kg, lying top up on the counter, its middle 42 cm forward and 38 cm right, its handle pointing toward the robot at right angles to the body handle: an oval aluminium plate 128 x 146 x 2.5 mm (4 mm larger than the mouth all round) edged with a 5 mm black rubber gasket, a vent tube in the middle, a 10 x 8 mm steel handle bar running 150 mm out from the vent tube to a 110 x 22 x 20 mm black bakelite lid handle (its end 25 mm past the body handle's when closed), and, hinged at the lid handle's end, a steel locking loop (3.5 mm wire, 44 mm wide, 60 mm long, 8 g) lying folded out on the counter. Seated, the lid's gasket is up against the underside of the rim's lip, the handle bar lies on the pivot, the lid handle sits 2 mm above the body handle, and the lid's top face is 4.5 mm below the rim's top; with nothing holding it the lid swings down into the cooker about the pivot. Real trial only: a thin film of cornflour-and-water paste wiped round the underside of the rim's lip, and four pieces of masking tape on the body just below the rim, on the mouth's diagonals (the depth marks). The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end, except the failures, which count at any time. Seated, four checks (real trial in brackets): (1) in line: the middle of the lid handle's end is within 13 mm sideways of the body handle's centre line (photo from above); (2) handles together: the lid handle's underside is within 4 mm of the body handle's top at the body handle's end (a 4 mm hex key cannot be pushed in between them there); (3) depth: at four points 5 mm in from the mouth's edge on its diagonals, the lid's top face is 4.5 +/- 2 mm below the rim's top (a caliper's depth rod at the four tape marks reads within 2 mm of D0, the depth read there once with the cooker closed by hand as the manual says; a photo of each reading); (4) witness ring: at 24 points round the gasket's outer edge, the gasket is at least 1 mm in under the rim and within 2 mm of its underside, and the lid touches the cooker (after opening, the cornflour paste has left an unbroken white ring at least 1 mm wide all round the black gasket; photo). Latched: the locking loop is swung in 34-50 degrees from hanging and its crossbar touches the cooker in the pocket under the body handle's end (photo: the loop over the handles' end, its crossbar under the body handle's end). Hands off: no finger pad touches the lid, the loop or the cooker, and each gripper is at least 5 cm from the lid handle's end and from the loop (video). Latch holds: 0.5 s after the hands are off a seated, latched lid, the lid handle is pulled straight up with 1 N, 10 mm in from its end, for 1 s, and every seated and latched check must hold throughout (a spring scale hooked there, pulled up to 100 g and held 1 s; the hex key still cannot go in; video). 1.0: seated, latched, hands off, and the latch held; 0.5: seated (e.g. the robot still holding the lid up); 0.25: the lid was at some time wholly inside the cooker, below the rim (video); else 0.0. 0.0 for good if at any time the cooker tips more than 25 degrees, or the cooker or the lid falls off the counter. An unlatched lid swings back into the cooker as soon as it is let go, so it cannot stay seated with the hands off; a lid that was seated and fell back fails checks 1-3 even if it left a ring. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the cooker, the lid and the loop still.
reset_notes: Open the cooker as the manual says (squeeze the handles, swing the loop out, push the lid toward the far wall and take it out the way it went in), wipe the gasket and the rim clean, wipe a fresh thin film of the cornflour paste round the underside of the rim's lip, and lay the lid top up on the counter at its marks, its handle toward the robot and the loop folded out. Rice and water: replace each session.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim, PhysX, 20 Hz). Real sizes; lid and mouth sizes are estimates; the 1.04 kg body is likely ~0.3 kg heavy (split from a carton weight). The gasket is rigid, where a real one is squeezed onto the rim: 'within 2 mm of the rim all round' stands for the witness ring, the catch is an arc-shaped pocket, and only pivot friction keeps the latched lid from sliding, so the latch-hold lift is 1 N. Bar rigid on the lid (real: some play). Rice and water: a rigid 0.40 kg layer.
